findings.claim: [15]'s fix joins a lost range into the last one only when the new range starts within the last or right at its end. A range that meets the last from below is kept apart, though it meets: (101,102) then (100,101). The count toward MaxRefusedRanges therefore depends on the order the file writes its subsections. A table losing 5,000 adjacent one-row subsections in ascending order keeps one range and reads normally. The same 5,000 in descending order make 5,000 ranges, refuse every number, and rebuild the whole file at opening. A stream's ranges (RefuseRanges) are sorted before they are joined, so they do not depend on order. The docs and the constant's comment say ranges that meet are joined as they are lost, which is false for this order. The cost is bounded but avoidable, and only a file that is not valid reaches it, as [15] was.
